Alex  thanks again for the discovery call earlier. Quick recap from our side and proposed next steps so we can lock the SLA/ops requirements into the mutual action plan.

Summary of what I heard you ask for:
- Latency targets: 95th percentile end-to-end for streaming responses <= 200ms (goal) / <= 300ms (acceptable).
- Throughput / concurrency: steady-state concurrency ~500 concurrent sessions, bursts up to ~1,000 concurrent sessions.
- Streaming: token-level streaming required (client consumes partial tokens) with low tail latency and ability to cancel streams quickly.
- Autoscale / burst: need burst capacity to handle 2x normal peak for up to 15 minutes without degraded P95 latency.
- Scale-up time expectation: ideally < 90s from burst detection to available capacity; preference for warm pool behavior to reduce cold start impact.

Open items we promised to follow up on:
1) Concrete scale-up timelines for the FastPay model profile (we'll share model load times and warm-pool options).
2) Queueing semantics and how we surface backpressure to the client vs. shedding.
3) Suggested warm pool sizing and a proposed scale-test plan.

Attachments: autoscale_slo_template.pdf (template we use to capture SLOs / measurement points). Also linking to the shared MOP: https://docs.google.com/document/d/1a2b-autoscale-slo-template

- P95 target: goal is 200ms for interactive flows (customer chat), acceptable up to 300ms for background tasks.
- Concurrency: 500 steady is correct; burst to 1,000 can happen in under 10 minutes (marketing campaigns). Bursts sometimes arrive as an ordered ramp (not instant).
- Streaming: yes, token-level streaming required. We also need ability to cancel streams from the client within 100ms of user action.

Questions:

2) For burst handling, would Redwood queue requests at the API gateway or return 429s when the queue exceeds the SLO window? We prefer a short queue with clear retry guidance vs opaque backpressure.

Hi Alex  thanks for the clarifying questions. Quick technical notes based on the model set we discussed and Redwood's autoscale options. High-level answers first, then details.

High-level:
- Recommended warm pool: for 13B quantized model -> reserve ~8-12 pre-warmed workers (GPUs) depending on request mix; for 70B fp16 -> reserve 2-3 warm workers if you expect occasional sessions. Warm instances keep model and KV cache resident to avoid model load + tokenizer warm-up.
- Model load times: typical 13B quantized cold load ~12-25s; 70B fp16 cold load ~25-60s depending on hardware and compilation cache. Warm transition (hot path) after warm pool hit is sub-second per new session.
- Scale-up latency: node provisioning + model load on a cold node ~30-90s; with warm pool this drops to nearly immediate availability for new sessions (<< 2s to accept requests).
- Queueing vs 429: we recommend a short bounded queue (configurable, default 200 requests) with transparent X-Redwood-Queue headers and retry-after guidance. For SLOs we can surface queue depth and estimated wait, and optionally fail fast with 429 when estimated wait exceeds the SLO window.

Details / configuration options:
1) Warm pool sizing: assume an average request uses 0.02 GPU-seconds per token generation (workload dependent). If you expect 500 concurrent interactive sessions with average response length 40 tokens, steady GPU concurrency estimate -> ~(500 * 40 * 0.02) = 400 GPU-seconds/s -> map to worker count by GPU throughput. We can run a profile with your sample prompts to get precise numbers.
2) Burst policy: we support a two-tier burst model: a) warm burst (use warm pool + burst capacity on same instance type) and b) cold burst (provision extra nodes in cloud pool). Warm burst handles short spikes (minutes) instantly; cold burst covers sustained increases but will have the scale-up latency above. You can set a maximum burst multiplier (e.g., 2x) and a time window before cold provisioning kicks in.
3) Observability: we emit token-level latency, queue depth, warm-pool hit rate, and P95/P99 per-route. We'll add sample Grafana dashboards for the sync.

Next steps I propose:
- Run a 30-minute synthetic burst test (we'll run from Redwood infra) using your sample prompt set to confirm warm pool sizing; deliverables: observed P95, queue depth, and warm-pool hit rate.
- If results look good, we capture recommended sizing in the autoscale_slo_template and put the values into the mutual action plan (HubSpot deal FP-2026-0457).

Attachment: scale_test_plan.xlsx (test cases and metrics).
